beats.narration_text: What's actually new in Kimi K3's architecture — and what does the 2.5× efficiency claim actually mean? 2.8 trillion parameters, 104 billion active. Two attention types. 896 experts. Each token picks 16. The rest sit idle. That's how you run a 3T-parameter brain at 100B-parameter cost.

props.headline: Vocabulary: 160K tokens. Context: 1,048,576. Vision encoder: MoonViT-V2.
props.body: Native multimodal — text and images in the same weights, no bolt-on adapter.

beats.narration_text: Vocabulary: 160K tokens. Context: 1,048,576. Vision encoder: MoonViT-V2. Native multimodal — text and images in the same weights, no bolt-on adapter.
93 layers. 69 run Kimi Delta Attention. 24 run Gated MLA. Two families. Both have a job.

graphic.mechanic: Big-O quadratic growth curve. X-axis: sequence length 0→1M tokens. Y-axis: compute ops (log scale). Red zone shaded past 1M tokens. Label: 'O(n²)'. Animate: curve sweeps left to right, red zone fills in at the end.

beats.narration_text: Standard attention scales as O(n²). A million tokens means a trillion attention operations per layer. Something has to give.
Delta attention is a hybrid. A linear recurrent pass — cheap, linear in n — is woven into the standard attention formula. Long context gets cheaper. Retrieval stays sharp.

beats.narration_text: Gated MLA compresses the KV cache. Instead of one key-value pair per head per layer, it stores a latent vector and decompresses at inference. That's how 1M context fits.

props.headline: NoPE: no positional encoding.
props.body: Standard rotary encodings anchor a model to training positions. Remove them and the model can extrapolate to context lengths it never saw.

beats.narration_text: NoPE: no positional encoding. Standard rotary encodings anchor a model to training positions. Remove them and the model can extrapolate to context lengths it never saw.

beats.narration_text: 69 cheap, long-range layers. 24 precise retrieval layers. Two axes, complementary strengths, one architecture.

props.headline: 2.5× scaling efficiency.
props.body: K3 reaches the same validation loss as K2 using 60% less compute. Read the curve on its own — it's a real gain.

beats.narration_text: 2.5× scaling efficiency: K3 reaches the same validation loss as K2 using 60% less compute. Read the curve on its own — it's a real gain.
Here's what rides on that single curve: a new attention architecture. Attention Residuals. A new load-balancing algorithm. And a new data recipe. Four changes. One measurement.

beats.narration_text: Attribution failure looks like this: combine four innovations, measure the combined gain, then write a headline about one of them. The figure doesn't support that headline. The headline is what gets remembered.
The load-balancing problem. 896 experts, most tokens route to a few popular ones. Those experts become bottlenecks. The others go idle. Wasted compute, wasted training.

props.headline: Why balance matters.
props.body: A 2.8T model with imbalanced expert loads wastes GPU time proportional to the load variance. Fix the balance and you recover that compute for actual learning.

beats.narration_text: Why balance matters: a 2.8T model with imbalanced expert loads wastes GPU time proportional to the load variance. Fix the balance and you recover that compute for actual learning.

graphic.mechanic: Before/after side-by-side bar charts. Left ('Before'): highly variable bar heights, variance gap labeled with bracket and 'Δ variance'. Right ('After'): bars near uniform height, variance bracket labeled 'Δ ≈ 0'. Caption: 'Balanced loading = recovered compute'. Colors: before bars #D97757; after bars #6fb0d6.

beats.narration_text: Before vs. after. Balanced loading changes training efficiency in a way you can measure. This is the most mechanistically transparent piece of the entire efficiency claim.

props.verdict: The 2.8T architecture is solid. The Stable LatentMoE design is well-documented and mechanistically coherent. The 2.5× efficiency number is plausible but causally opaque — it bundles four changes without isolating any. The validation loss is a private metric, not a downstream capability score. When someone cites the 2.5×: 'the full redesign together is ~2.5× more efficient than K2.' Never attribute it to one component.

Verdict. Two Axes, One Curve. The architecture is real innovation: KDA combined with FullAttRes in one model, Latent MoE with a pooled capacity quota, and a two-stage training recipe. The two-point-five times fewer FLOPs claim bundles all four changes into one headline. The attribution figure in the paper does not support the claim that KDA alone delivered the efficiency gain. Architecture: genuine. Efficiency attribution: unsupported. The innovations are meaningful — the specific credit allocation is not.

Your turn. Ask Claude to explain KDA — Knowledge-Distilled Attention — and what problem it solves at inference time. Then ask Kimi K3 the same question. Compare which answer is more specific about the trade-off between training cost and inference cost. Watch for either model conflating fewer parameters with fewer FLOPs.
